summary:
Bayelsa State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework on sexual orientation and gender identity, and no state-specific enforcement divergence is documented for it. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. It renders any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void, bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and reaches participants and guests at same-sex weddings, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across Nigeria since 1916.

The maximum penalty for same-sex sexual activity in Bayelsa is 14 years' imprisonment. The death penalty is confined to the twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes and does not reach Bayelsa. Those codes carry penalties ranging from lashes or caning to death by stoning: a Shari'a court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and a further death-by-stoning sentence was reported from Bauchi in May 2024. In January 2014 a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial.

Arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people are recorded countrywide in the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025, which documents the national framework applying across all states. Police have used the 2014 statute to justify torture and arbitrary arrest, according to Human Rights Watch (October 2016). Enforcement in practice is frequently extractive: in March 2025 TimesLIVE reported that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised under the national statute, but gender expression carries exposure. Nigeria offers no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advisory, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in the states that operate it. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 statute reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye). She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, and served it in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Two legal layers coexist inside one country, and the difference between them is the difference between a long prison term and execution. Bayelsa sits in the secular southern half, where the ceiling is 14 years; the twelve Shari'a states carry stoning provisions that have been imposed at least twice in Bauchi since 2022. A visitor crossing state lines inside Nigeria changes criminal regime without changing country.

The recorded violence pattern is national rather than local, and it runs ahead of the statute. The killing of Abuja Area Mama in August 2024, the beating and extortion of Okafor in Lagos in March 2025, and the kito gang operations documented in April 2024 are three separate mechanisms producing harm against people perceived as LGBT+, none of which required a completed prosecution under the 2014 Act.

The advisory environment has tightened in step with the reporting. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's warning, carried by Sahara Reporters in August 2026, names arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation together, and adds the specific and unusual point that participants and guests at same-sex weddings are themselves criminalised.

Where a state-level record is absent, the absence is itself the finding: no Bayelsa-specific incident series, protective statute or enforcement pattern appears in these sources, so any assessment of the state rests on the national framework plus national violence data.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bayelsa live under the secular national penal code, not Shari'a law, so exposure for same-sex conduct is imprisonment of up to 14 years rather than corporal or capital punishment. The twelve Shari'a states' codes do not extend here.

Nigeria provides residents with no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection and no recognition of same-sex relationships. A trans person has no statutory basis on which to claim a partner, a household, or protection at work or in services.

Housing placement in custody is decided by prison authorities rather than by rule. In the Bobrisky case the October 2024 panel found that keeping a first-time offender in a maximum-security prison breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, but the finding concerned the class of prison, not whether a trans woman is housed with men or women.

Police contact carries a direct financial and physical risk for people read as gay or trans. The Lagos case in March 2025 shows extraction as the operative logic: a beating followed by a reduced bribe payment, with release contingent on cash.

The 2014 statute reaches into private association. Cohabitation with a same-sex partner, organising or joining a gay organisation, and attending a same-sex wedding are all offences in their own right, so a resident's social and domestic arrangements carry criminal exposure independent of sexual conduct.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is unresolved in these sources. The current status of any such provision in Bayelsa is not sourced here.

No Bayelsa-specific enforcement data appears in the inventory: no arrest counts, prosecution figures, state police directives or reported incidents attributable to the state are documented, and the absence is not evidence that enforcement does or does not occur.

Document and marker rules for trans visitors, entry and exit screening practices, and access to transition-related healthcare are not covered by any source supplied for this record, and remain unverified.

The relationship between the 10-year and 14-year figures for the 2014 Act is carried from Human Rights Watch as a range; the inventory does not identify which offence carries which term.

The bribery allegations against those who arranged Bobrisky's prison treatment were dismissed by the October 2024 investigative panel; the panel's separate finding on the illegality of her maximum-security housing is the only substantiated outcome recorded here.

Charges in the killing of Abuja Area Mama remain unresolved as of the February 2025 reporting; later developments are not sourced.
